edition.title: P100 NEWS + CULTURE + SCIENCE & TECH + SPORT
edition.deck: A deadly strike in Ukraine, a legal setback for Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor and growing pressure on public services lead today’s coverage.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises consequential developments and original reporting. Related coverage of the same events is combined where it adds useful detail; allegations and contested claims remain attributed.

content.headline: Russian strike on Kramatorsk buses kills at least 30, officials say
content.shortHeadline: Strike on Kramatorsk buses kills at least 30
content.standfirst: The attack on civilian buses in the eastern Ukrainian city also wounded 18, officials say. It comes amid a sharp increase in Russian attacks and civilian casualties across the country.

image.caption: A damaged bus after the strike in Kramatorsk.

sources.originalTitle: Russian strike on buses kills at least 30, say officials, as deadly attacks on Ukraine surge
Russian attack on bus kills at least 30 people near Ukraine frontline

segments.body: At least 30 people were killed and 18 wounded when a Russian aerial bomb hit buses in Kramatorsk, Ukrainian officials said. A second bus caught fire. Authorities also reported three people killed in nearby Bilenke and ordered public transport in the area to stop.

segments.title: Attacks intensify
segments.body: Kramatorsk and nearby Sloviansk form part of a Ukrainian-held area of Donetsk that Russia is seeking to capture. The strike followed an attack on an apartment block in Pryluky that killed at least 22 people, including five children. Moscow had not commented on the Kramatorsk strike in the reporting gathered.

content.headline: Gaza civilians still face Israeli strikes as ceasefire plan stalls
content.shortHeadline: Israeli strikes continue in Gaza as peace plan stalls
content.standfirst: Palestinians describe displacement, precarious shelter and ongoing danger a year after a ceasefire began. The deal’s next phase, including reconstruction, remains stalled.

image.caption: Fida al-Toutah’s family say she was killed by gunfire in their tent.

sources.originalTitle: 'Every day there is killing': Gazans face Israeli strikes despite ceasefire as peace deal stalls

segments.body: Israeli attacks have continued in Gaza despite the ceasefire that began on 10 October last year. Gaza’s Hamas-run health ministry says more than 1,400 people have been killed in attacks since then; the ministry’s figures are considered reliable by the UN. Israel says it targets Hamas and accuses the group of violating the ceasefire.

segments.title: Life in displacement
segments.body: Families interviewed by the BBC described repeated moves, unsafe tents and the struggle to secure food, water and warmth. The BBC reported that Israel’s military said it had no record of the incidents in which Fida al-Toutah and 14-year-old Ismail al-Bardawil were killed.

segments.title: A stalled next phase
segments.body: Reconstruction has not begun as the parties remain at odds over the next stage of the deal. Israel says it will not withdraw until Hamas is disarmed; Hamas says disarmament depends on Israel ending its attacks and withdrawing. The US recovery plan has also made little progress, the BBC reports.

content.headline: El Niño strengthens as droughts, fires and floods hit several regions
content.shortHeadline: Strengthening El Niño brings drought, fires and floods
content.standfirst: New measurements show warmer-than-usual Pacific waters, while forecasters say the climate pattern is likely to strengthen further. Its effects are already being reported across several regions.

image.caption: A service in El Salvador calls for rain amid drought linked to El Niño.

sources.originalTitle: Nye tal: El Niño vokser sig stadig kraftigere - og i disse lande rammer den allerede hårdt

segments.body: The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration measured central Pacific sea temperatures 2.1C above normal in September, up from 1.8C in August. NOAA put the chance of this becoming the strongest El Niño recorded since 1950 at 83%; the World Meteorological Organization expects it to persist at least until February 2027.

segments.title: Uneven effects
segments.body: The report links El Niño to drought affecting crops in Central America and India, fires in Indonesia and unusually wet conditions in parts of Japan. The World Food Programme warns the pattern could push at least 49 million more people into acute hunger by the end of 2027.

content.headline: Alberta voters face first step towards a possible independence vote
content.shortHeadline: Alberta vote tests support for a future independence referendum
content.standfirst: The 19 October ballot asks whether Alberta should move towards a binding referendum on independence, not whether to leave Canada now. The economic costs and benefits are disputed.

image.caption: Alberta voters will decide whether to advance towards an independence referendum.

sources.originalTitle: How oil-rich Alberta's economy might fare if it broke away from Canada

segments.body: Albertans will vote on 19 October on whether to stay in Canada or proceed to a later, binding independence referendum. Supporters argue the oil-rich province contributes more to federal finances than it receives; opponents warn that separation could bring major costs, lost investment and trade uncertainty.

segments.title: Competing cost estimates
segments.body: A report commissioned by Premier Danielle Smith’s government estimates separation could cost C$50bn–C$170bn over five years. A separate CanadaWest Foundation report estimates Alberta could take on C$258bn–C$333bn in additional debt. The pro-independence Alberta Prosperity Project forecasts a large annual surplus, but economists cited by the BBC question its assumptions.

content.headline: US prosecutors add torture-conspiracy charges against Nicolás Maduro
content.shortHeadline: Maduro faces new US torture-conspiracy charges
content.standfirst: The new accusations concern US citizens allegedly tortured while held in Venezuela. Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, deny earlier drug and weapons charges; their trial is set for June 2027.

image.caption: Nicolás Maduro has been in US custody since January.

sources.originalTitle: Venezuela's ex-leader Nicolás Maduro charged with conspiracy to commit torture
Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro expected to face more charges this week

segments.body: US prosecutors have accused former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, of conspiring to commit torture against US citizens detained in Venezuela while he was in power. The charges are additional to existing drug-trafficking and weapons accusations, which the couple deny.
Maduro and Flores have been in US custody since January, after US forces seized them in a raid in Caracas and brought them to Brooklyn. Their trial is scheduled to begin in June 2027.

content.headline: French school protests inspire demonstrations across Europe
content.shortHeadline: French school protests spur demonstrations elsewhere in Europe
content.standfirst: Students in France are protesting school conditions and funding; demonstrations have also emerged in other countries, with participants citing the French movement as an influence.

image.caption: A demonstration outside a school in Nantes, western France.

sources.originalTitle: France's school protests: What lies behind the anger
Unges protester inspirerer: 'Lad os gøre som i Frankrig'

segments.body: French pupils have protested over staff shortages, run-down buildings and long school days. Demonstrations have sometimes turned violent, with injuries and arrests reported. The BBC notes that France spends more per upper-secondary pupil than the EU average, and that some complaints do not fully explain the scale of the unrest.

perspectives.body: DR reports that students in Belgium, Italy and Greece have also mobilised, citing issues including worn-out schools, crowded classes and education costs. Some participants say the French protests have inspired them, though the demands differ between countries.

segments.title: A tradition of protest
segments.body: In France, student demonstrations have previously won spending and policy changes, including school renovations and extra staff. The current movement is unfolding amid political gridlock and tight public finances, factors that could limit the government’s ability to respond.

content.headline: Christa Pike walks in hospital after botched Tennessee execution
content.shortHeadline: Christa Pike walks after failed execution; next steps unclear
content.standfirst: Pike is recovering after surviving two lethal-injection doses, her legal team says. Tennessee has paused executions while it investigates, and lawyers are seeking a commutation.

image.caption: Christa Pike at a court hearing in Knoxville, Tennessee, in 2007.

sources.originalTitle: Christa Pike now walking after failed US execution, lawyer tells BBC
Christa Pike is ‘up and walking’ for first time after failed execution, lawyer says
Could Christa Pike face execution again and by what method?

segments.body: Christa Pike is walking short distances around her hospital room, though her arms remain badly injured and she is mentally foggy, her lawyer Stephen Ferrell told the BBC. Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital during an execution attempt on 30 September.

segments.title: What happens next
segments.body: A judge has ordered Tennessee officials to preserve evidence from the execution attempt. Governor Bill Lee has paused executions for the rest of the year and ordered an investigation. Pike’s lawyers are seeking life without parole; the state has not said whether it will try again, and legal experts cited by the BBC describe significant hurdles to another lethal injection.

content.headline: Tracked wildlife populations have fallen 73% since 1970, WWF report says
content.shortHeadline: WWF says monitored wildlife populations have fallen 73%
content.standfirst: The Living Planet report finds steep declines across monitored animal populations, while also documenting recovery in some. The headline figure measures population change, not the share of species lost.

image.caption: Wild tiger populations have increased, according to the report.

source.credit: Foto: Kazakhstans Ministry Of Ecology And Natural Resources / Ritzau Scanpix

sources.originalTitle: Direktør slår alarm over ny rapport om vilde dyr

segments.body: WWF’s Living Planet report says monitored wild-animal populations worldwide have declined by 73% since 1970. It analysed 35,803 populations across 5,790 species. Habitat loss and degradation are identified as the largest threats, alongside climate change, overexploitation, pollution, invasive species and disease.

segments.title: Some populations recover
segments.body: The report says 43% of monitored populations are increasing, including wild tiger numbers, which it estimates rose 70% from 2010 to 2025. WWF points to conservation measures and community involvement as factors in some recoveries.

content.headline: Court rules warrants for Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor searches unlawful
content.shortHeadline: Andrew search warrants ruled unlawful; police inquiry continues
content.standfirst: Thames Valley Police accepted that the warrants were issued under the wrong legal provision. The ruling quashes them, but does not end the investigation or settle whether police can retain seized material.

image.caption: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor remains under police investigation after the warrants ruling.

sources.originalTitle: Police accept Andrew search warrants were unlawful, court hears
Search warrants used in Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor raids were unlawful, court rules

segments.body: The High Court ruled that search warrants used at Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor’s homes were unlawful after Thames Valley Police accepted that the wrong provision of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act had been used. The searches followed his February arrest on suspicion of misconduct in public office, which he denies.

segments.title: Investigation remains open
segments.body: The judge quashed the warrants but said that this did not invalidate the entire investigation. Police have applied to retain the documents and electronic devices seized during the searches; the court is expected to hear that application next year. The force says the legal ruling concerns the warrants’ legal basis, not its ongoing inquiry.

content.headline: Royal Navy sailor charged with preparing to pass secrets to Russia
content.shortHeadline: Navy sailor charged over alleged plans to pass secrets to Russia
content.standfirst: Teddy Young, 24, is accused of obtaining protected information and drafting a Russian-language message containing classified material. He has been remanded in custody and has not entered a plea in the reporting gathered.

image.caption: Teddy Young appears at Westminster Magistrates’ Court.

sources.originalTitle: Royal Navy sailor appears in court charged with spying for Russia

segments.body: A serving Royal Navy intelligence rating has been charged under the National Security Act with offences relating to protected information. Prosecutors allege that Teddy Young prepared to disclose information to benefit a foreign power and drafted a message in Russian containing classified material.

Young was arrested at his Bedfordshire home and remanded in custody, with a further hearing scheduled at the Old Bailey for 16 October. Counter Terrorism Policing London said it had worked with the Ministry of Defence to mitigate possible risks. The case is not connected to the separate RAF Fairford investigation.

content.headline: Potentially harmful PFAS chemical found at almost all English water sites tested
content.shortHeadline: PFAS chemical found at nearly all English water sites tested
content.standfirst: Environment Agency tests detected trifluoroacetic acid in every surface-water site and most groundwater sites sampled. Its health risks are still being studied, and England has no limit for the chemical in water.

image.caption: The River Ancholme had the highest TFA concentration recorded in surface water.

sources.originalTitle: Forever chemical linked to fertility issues found in rivers in England

segments.body: Environment Agency tests at 99 English water sites in 2024 found trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) in all 50 surface-water samples and 43 of 49 groundwater samples. TFA is a persistent PFAS chemical; two-fifths of tested surface-water sites were above the EU’s new limit for PFAS in rivers and lakes if TFA were the only PFAS present.

segments.title: Health questions remain
segments.body: The European Chemicals Agency has recommended classifying TFA as a presumed reproductive toxicant, based on animal testing; human effects remain under study. A scientist cited in the report said current levels are not necessarily high enough to cause health problems but warned that levels appear to be rising. The UK has no TFA water limit, and a drinking-water risk programme is due to report next year.

content.headline: BBC apologises and pays compensation over false PinkNews allegations
content.shortHeadline: BBC pays compensation over false allegations about PinkNews couple
content.standfirst: The broadcaster admitted that a documentary and accompanying article made false and defamatory claims about Benjamin Cohen and Anthony James. The couple say the damage extended to their family and work.

image.caption: Benjamin Cohen and Anthony James in London in 2022.

sources.originalTitle: BBC pays compensation to PinkNews couple over false sexual misconduct allegations

segments.body: The BBC has apologised and agreed to pay substantial compensation to PinkNews founder Benjamin Cohen and his husband, Anthony James. At the High Court, it accepted that a 2024 documentary and related article made false and defamatory allegations of sexual misconduct and inappropriate pressure on staff.

The couple said the claims led to professional consequences and additional investigations by family authorities before a hearing concerning their son. They said the BBC had ignored warnings about the allegations’ accuracy. The corporation retracted and apologised for the claims; the programme and article have been removed.

content.headline: Staff shortages threaten promised specialist support for pupils with SEND
content.shortHeadline: Staff shortages threaten specialist support for pupils with SEND
content.standfirst: The government’s £1.8bn Experts at Hand programme aims to bring specialists into mainstream schools, but councils and sector groups warn that recruitment gaps could limit delivery. Ministers say rollout is only beginning.

image.caption: Schools minister Georgia Gould announced the Experts at Hand scheme.

sources.originalTitle: SEND pupils’ extra support at risk with schools unable to access specialist staff

segments.body: The Experts at Hand scheme is intended to improve mainstream pupils’ access to educational psychologists, speech and language therapists, occupational therapists and specialist teachers. At least 36 councils have raised concerns about staffing, according to analysis by Schools Week cited by the i Paper.

segments.title: Capacity is the test
segments.body: Sector groups say shortages and recruitment pressures may leave families expecting help that is not available. An Education Policy Institute report cited in the article estimated that about 1,400 additional full-time-equivalent educational psychologists were needed across nearly 100 council areas. The Department for Education says the three-year programme is being phased in and that workforce capacity will take time to build.

content.headline: Nursery staff face proposed phone and photo restrictions in safeguarding plan
content.shortHeadline: Nursery staff face proposed phone and photo restrictions
content.standfirst: Draft guidance would restrict personal devices in childcare areas and limit routine photographs of children. The plans follow abuse and data-security cases; staff representatives say training and staffing will also matter.

image.caption: Proposed guidance would restrict digital devices in childcare settings.

sources.originalTitle: Nursery staff to be banned from using phones after ‘chilling’ child abuse case

segments.body: Government guidance expected this month would tell nursery staff, childminders and visitors not to use personal phones or digital devices in childcare areas. Staff would use a designated work device, with photographs subject to parental consent and checks by supervisors, according to sources familiar with the plans cited by the i Paper.

segments.title: Safeguarding and practical concerns
segments.body: The proposed rules follow the case of a nursery worker jailed for abusing children and a separate cyberattack involving children’s images. The guidance is expected to limit routine photographs and warn against posting identifiable images online. A union representative cautioned that shortages and high staff turnover could make consistent safeguarding difficult.

content.headline: Paramount-Warner Bros merger raises UK concerns over media choice and news
content.shortHeadline: Media merger raises UK concerns over competition and news independence
content.standfirst: The combined company will own Channel 5 and a large portfolio of UK television and streaming services. The merger was approved with conditions, including continued free-to-air Channel 5 and editorial independence for its news operation until 2034.

image.caption: Paramount and Warner Bros are now part of the same company.

sources.originalTitle: The world has a new media giant and it wants more hobbits and Harry Potter

segments.body: Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros Discovery have completed a merger that brings Channel 5, CNN, TNT Sports and other services under one company. UK government analysis cited by the i Paper estimated their combined linear-TV viewing share at 12%, making them the country’s third-largest broadcaster by that measure.

segments.title: Questions over influence and jobs
segments.body: UK approval came with conditions, including that Channel 5 remain a free-to-air public broadcaster until at least 2034 and its news arm remain editorially independent from CBS and CNN during that period. The new owners are targeting $6bn in savings; the company says most would not come from job losses, while media analyst David Folkenflik warned that the merger could reduce choice and increase prices.

content.headline: Conservatives favour social-care cost cap over Labour’s proposed service
content.shortHeadline: Tories weigh social-care cost cap against Labour’s care plan
content.standfirst: A senior Conservative source says the party is drawn to a lifetime cap to limit the need to sell family homes, rejecting a free-at-the-point-of-use National Care Service. The details and funding remain unsettled.

image.caption: Kemi Badenoch at the Conservative Party conference.

sources.originalTitle: Tories to revive plans for social care cap – and reject Burnham pledge

segments.body: The Conservatives are considering a lifetime cap on social-care costs, after which the state would pay the remaining care costs, according to a senior party source cited by the i Paper. The approach differs from Andy Burnham’s proposed National Care Service, which would be free at the point of use.

segments.title: Funding and eligibility unresolved
segments.body: A cap could reduce pressure on some families to sell their homes, but its level would determine how much protection it offers. The government’s proposed free personal care would initially cover only people aged 65 and over, leaving working-age disabled adults outside that commitment. The parties’ funding proposals and wider reforms remain contested.

content.headline: CPR leak prompts surge in credit warnings, but protection is limited
content.shortHeadline: Credit warnings surge after CPR leak, but are not full protection
content.standfirst: About 970,000 people had a credit warning by 7 October, up from nearly 250,000 before the leak of 8.8 million CPR numbers was reported. A warning can help guard against identity misuse but may make borrowing harder.

image.caption: A credit warning asks lenders to take extra care before granting credit in someone’s name.

sources.originalTitle: Kreditadvarsel er ekstra sikring - men det kan skabe falsk tryghed
700.000 danskere opretter kreditadvarsel efter CPR-læk

segments.body: The number of people registered with a credit warning rose to about 970,000 by 7 October, from nearly 250,000 on 1 October, according to figures from the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalisation. The increase followed the disclosure that 8.8 million CPR numbers had been exposed.

segments.title: Use with care
segments.body: A warning flags to lenders that they should take extra care before granting credit, but it can also make loans or credit harder to obtain. Consumer Council Tænk says it is an extra safeguard, not a guarantee against fraud. The minister advises people to consider one if they have concrete reason to suspect misuse.

content.headline: Former prison officer describes violence and pressure in Danish jails
content.shortHeadline: Former officer alleges violence inside overstretched Danish prisons
content.standfirst: Kim Knudsen says years in a high-security unit left him with PTSD and describes violence by staff and prisoners. Prison authorities say the account is new to them and that allegations of staff violence are acted on.

image.caption: Prison staff and inmates work and live within the same secure environment.

sources.originalTitle: Tidligere fængselsbetjent afslører gensidig voldelig kultur

segments.body: Former prison officer Kim Knudsen says he developed PTSD after two decades in a high-security unit, where he experienced threats and violence. In a new book, he alleges that officers assaulted prisoners, coordinated accounts and lied in use-of-force reports. These are his allegations; prison authorities say they had not previously heard this account.

segments.title: Pressure on the system
segments.body: The Prison Officers’ Union says Denmark has 4,650 prisoners for 4,300 places, alongside a historically low number of officers. Prison Service director Ina Eliasen called Knudsen’s description extremely serious and said the service takes action, including reporting staff to police, when it learns of violence against prisoners.

content.headline: South Korean shipbuilder excluded from Denmark’s frigate competition
content.shortHeadline: South Korean frigate offer excluded from Danish competition
content.standfirst: HD Hyundai says it could build Denmark’s new frigates faster and for less than European rivals, but a prior political agreement limits the competition to European Nato countries. Experts differ on the strategic trade-offs.

image.caption: South Korean frigate Jeongjo the Great was delivered to the South Korean navy in 2024.

sources.originalTitle: Skal Danmark købe krigsskibe af Sydkorea? Her er fordelene og ulemperne ved slagtilbuddet

segments.body: South Korea’s HD Hyundai Heavy Industries will not be allowed to submit a formal offer for Denmark’s new frigates because the political agreement governing the purchase specifies a European Nato supplier. The company has said its ships could be 20–30% cheaper than European alternatives and delivered faster.

segments.title: Cost versus cooperation
segments.body: Experts cited by DR say a Nato supplier could offer closer cooperation on training, maintenance and spare parts. One former admiral argues the South Korean offer should still be considered and could strengthen Denmark’s negotiating position; another analyst points to the security relationship Denmark already has with European Nato allies.

content.headline: Denmark changes coastal-protection rules to prioritise people and nature
content.shortHeadline: New coastal rules prioritise people and nature over property values
content.standfirst: The government and a broad parliamentary majority will change how state coastal-protection funds are allocated. The revised criteria give greater weight to people, natural barriers and cultural heritage, while experts warn the available funding cannot protect every home.

image.caption: Faxe Ladeplads was flooded during a storm surge in 2023.

sources.originalTitle: Helt nye regler ved kysterne kan presse danskere fra deres hjem

segments.body: State support for coastal-protection projects will no longer be prioritised mainly according to property values, the government and a broad parliamentary majority have agreed. New criteria will give greater weight to protecting people, nature-based projects and cultural heritage, with changes phased in during 2026 and 2027.

segments.title: Some places may remain exposed
segments.body: The coastal fund is expected to provide 800 million kroner over four years, but a climate professor cited by TV 2 says that will not protect every home and that some people may eventually need to move inland. The new approach follows criticism that Faxe Ladeplads was denied support under the previous rules, which gave weight to local house prices.

content.headline: Fewer Chinese parcels recorded in Denmark, but deliveries barely fall
content.shortHeadline: Temu parcels still reach Denmark despite sharp customs-data fall
content.standfirst: Customs records show a 99.5% drop in low-value imports after new EU rules, but parcel carrier dao reports only a 3–5% fall in deliveries. The difference suggests many shipments are now cleared elsewhere in Europe.

sources.originalTitle: Minister jubler over vildt fald i Temu-pakker – men branchefolk fortæller en anden historie

segments.body: Danish customs records fell from as many as 2.2 million low-value parcels a week to fewer than 10,000 after new EU rules removed the exemption from duties on goods worth under €150. Tax and growth minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt called the change a major success.

segments.title: The route has changed
segments.body: Parcel carrier dao says deliveries of Chinese goods fell only 3–5% compared with the same period last year, and that parcels now arrive by truck from elsewhere in Europe rather than through Danish airports. Business groups say purchases continue and argue that sellers should be held to the same product-safety rules as Danish retailers. Customs says it is monitoring the change and that it is too early to assess its structural effect.

content.headline: Climate Council urges Denmark to raise taxes on air travel
content.shortHeadline: Climate Council calls for higher Danish air-travel taxes
content.standfirst: The council says the passenger levy should rise from 50 to 170 kroner for trips to other EU countries by 2030. A government party representative warns higher national charges could push travellers to depart from other countries.

image.caption: Copenhagen Airport recorded 9.9 million passengers in June, July and August.

sources.originalTitle: Klimarådet vil gøre det dyrere for danskerne at flyve

segments.body: The Danish Climate Council recommends raising passenger taxes as air travel grows and the sector pays relatively little for its emissions. It says the charge on travel to other EU countries, scheduled to reach 50 kroner in 2030, should instead be 170 kroner.

segments.title: Concern about displacement
segments.body: Moderates energy spokesperson Lars Aagaard opposes a higher Danish levy, warning that travellers could drive to Hamburg or Malmö or fly from Stockholm instead. The council acknowledges that some climate benefit could be lost if passengers shift their departure points abroad; Aagaard argues the issue is better addressed at EU level.

content.headline: Man jailed for threatening Odense councillor online
content.shortHeadline: Man jailed for threats against Odense councillor
content.standfirst: A man has received three months in prison for threats against councillor Signe Vedersø Keldorff on social media. She says intimidation can discourage people from entering politics.

image.caption: Odense councillor Signe Vedersø Keldorff welcomed the sentence.

sources.originalTitle: Mand skal i fængsel for trusler mod byrådspolitiker

segments.body: A man has been sentenced to three months’ unconditional imprisonment for threatening Odense city councillor Signe Vedersø Keldorff on social media after she posted on TikTok. She welcomed the sentence and thanked Funen Police for its work on the case.

Keldorff says threats and harassment can deter people interested in politics from becoming candidates or taking part in public life. She hopes the sentence reinforces that political debate must remain open to everyone.

content.headline: Kolding family disputes cut to support for care of disabled daughter
content.shortHeadline: Family challenges council’s cut to care support for disabled child
content.standfirst: Kolding Municipality says the mother’s business and Instagram growth are relevant to its decision to reduce compensation for lost earnings. The family disputes that assessment and has appealed.

sources.originalTitle: Mors Instagram er skyld i manglende støtte til pasning af sygt barn, skriver kommune

segments.body: Sofie Bregnhøj Suhr says Kolding Municipality used the growth of her Instagram account and income from a small business when reducing her compensation for lost earnings while caring for her daughter Molly, who has a rare skull condition. The municipality says it must respond to new information that may affect a benefit decision.

segments.title: Dispute over what the evidence shows
segments.body: Suhr says her account was growing before the family appeared in a television documentary and that her business earns about 3,000 kroner a month. A legal specialist quoted by TV Syd argues the business is not equivalent to the full-time job Suhr gave up to care for Molly. The family has appealed to the Appeals Board.

content.headline: The Avalanches turn jingles, old tech and memory into a new pop odyssey
content.shortHeadline: The Avalanches build an album around memory and old technology
content.standfirst: On No Bad Memories, the sample-driven Australian trio turn computer sounds, jingles and fragments of pop into a frenetic new record—and made a companion film with Haley Joel Osment.

image.caption: The Avalanches’ Robbie Chater, who says their sampled sounds hold memories and human feeling.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Spend time going down rabbit holes’: how the Avalanches created their wildest album yet

segments.title: A record that skips ahead
segments.body: The Avalanches’ new album, No Bad Memories, draws on the sounds of advertising and outdated technology: jingles, audio logos, computer drones and video-game bleeps. Robbie Chater and Tony Di Blasi say they wanted something brighter and more playful than their previous record, shaping the songs to move on abruptly, as if the listener were skipping through a playlist.

segments.title: A world built from samples
segments.body: The record’s musical palette reaches from children’s science television to Tunisian footwork, with guests including John Glacier, Khadija Al Hanafi, Panda Bear and Haruomi Hosono. The band say clearing samples has become increasingly difficult and costly; after finishing the album, they swore off the process—then immediately started sampling again.

segments.title: The film beside the album
segments.body: A 35-minute companion film, directed by the Avalanches with Jonathan Zawada, stars Haley Joel Osment as an employee of a fictional digital archive. The story follows him as he collects people’s possessions and begins to lose track of which memories are his and which have been shaped by the advertisements he has absorbed.

content.headline: Helen’s new album finds Liz Harris making room for friendship and noise
content.shortHeadline: Helen’s Linda’s Head makes room for Liz Harris to sing out
content.standfirst: Grouper’s Liz Harris returns with her dream-pop trio Helen, whose second album brings her lyrics forward without losing its enveloping sound. The band’s collaborators describe the collective process as restorative.

image.caption: Liz Harris of Helen and Grouper.

sources.originalTitle: Linda’s Head
‘It’s rational to fear the music industry’: Grouper’s Liz Harris on virality, streaming scammers and her ‘restorative’ dream-pop trio

segments.body: Linda’s Head, the second album by Helen, gives Liz Harris’s voice and lyrics more definition than the trio’s 2015 debut. Pitchfork hears a set of concise phrases and vivid images—stars, storms and horizons—inside music that still swells and engulfs the listener. Its review finds the group’s increased clarity does not diminish shoegaze’s enveloping force.

perspectives.body: In an interview, Harris describes Helen as a welcome contrast to Grouper’s solitary process: playing with friends lets her show a more playful side, and rehearsals helped lift her spirits while she was dealing with medical difficulties.

segments.title: The risk of being heard
segments.body: The album’s brighter moments sit beside its darkness, including songs prompted by a dead shark Harris saw on the coast. Harris also discusses the risks of a sudden online audience: a fraudulent upload of her song “Poison Tree” reportedly earned around six figures before she and her label shut the scam down and recovered what she was owed.

content.headline: Jamie T looks back on his early career—and the cost of touring Europe
content.shortHeadline: Jamie T reflects on 20 years of music and costly touring
content.standfirst: The singer-songwriter’s new album revisits the music and anxieties of his early career. He says the expense of touring with a band means he can no longer make European dates work financially.

image.caption: Jamie T, whose album Ghosts (100 Days of Morning) looks back on his career.

sources.originalTitle: Jamie T: ‘I can’t afford to tour Europe anymore’

segments.body: Jamie T’s sixth album, Ghosts (100 Days of Morning), looks back on the period when he began making music as a teenager. He says he wanted to bring that chapter to a close and move on. The song “Tallahassee” folds references to Paul Heaton, Lily Allen and Liam Howlett into a reflection on the moments that made an artist’s life feel iconic.

segments.title: A career shaped by anxiety
segments.body: Treays describes panic disorder as a constant difficulty during his early touring years. He still experiences anxiety, he says, but not at the same intensity. He also recalls how the pressure of a major hometown show prompted him to write, turning self-doubt into the starting point for “Tallahassee.”

segments.title: The economics of getting on the road
segments.body: The musician says ticket sales are his main source of income, but touring with a band is expensive. He has not toured Europe since Brexit, and says the numbers do not currently add up for a run of dates there. He would like to take the new album beyond the UK, but is frustrated that doing so is not financially viable.

content.headline: Interpol find new colours in their eighth album, This Mirror Weighs a Ton
content.shortHeadline: Interpol reshape their sound on This Mirror Weighs a Ton
content.standfirst: After years in the shadow of their early records, Interpol say new collaborators and a return to writing in New York helped open fresh paths on their eighth album.

image.caption: Interpol’s Paul Banks and Daniel Kessler.

sources.originalTitle: Interpol: ‘People romanticise the Noughties music scene. We weren’t all friends’

segments.body: This Mirror Weighs a Ton keeps Interpol’s angular guitars and tense post-punk, while opening space for piano ballads, woodwind, glockenspiel and, for the first time, acoustic guitar. The band’s Paul Banks and Daniel Kessler call the album a product of new creative choices, including bringing touring bassist Brad Truax into the writing process and working closely with producer Andrew Wyatt.

segments.title: A return to familiar ground
segments.body: Writing and recording in New York for the first time since 2014 brought the band back to places tied to their early history. Banks and Kessler also reflect on the much-romanticised New York indie scene of the early 2000s: they remember sharing clubs with other bands, but say the idea that everyone was close friends was not quite true.

segments.title: Art, technology and sincerity
segments.body: Banks says he is sceptical of using AI to make art for the sake of selling it, while Kessler says listeners remain curious about the person and choices behind a piece of music. The album’s lyrics also engage with contemporary unease, including Banks’s response to graphic footage of war he encountered online.

content.headline: Soft Cell’s final album becomes a closing chapter after Dave Ball’s death
content.shortHeadline: Soft Cell’s Danceteria is a final album after Dave Ball’s death
content.standfirst: Marc Almond says he will not make another Soft Cell record without his longtime bandmate. Their newly released album revisits the duo’s formative New York years and the club culture that shaped them.

image.caption: Soft Cell’s Marc Almond and Dave Ball.

sources.originalTitle: Soft Cell’s Marc Almond: ‘We finished the album – two days later Dave passed away’

segments.body: Soft Cell had finished Danceteria when keyboardist Dave Ball died in his sleep in October 2025, two days after he and Marc Almond agreed the record was complete. Almond calls it the duo’s sixth and final album, saying he would not make another Soft Cell record without Ball. He remembers feeling numb when he heard the news.

segments.title: New York remembered
segments.body: The album looks back to the pair’s time in New York in the early 1980s, especially the club Danceteria. Almond describes the city’s underground nightlife as exhilarating and creative, but also lonely and increasingly shadowed by the AIDS crisis. The record balances dance-pop celebrations with songs about isolation, escape and regret.

segments.title: An ending they made together
segments.body: Almond says the pair had grown closer while making the album, and that finishing it together feels like a fitting way to close their shared musical story. Their final concert was at the Rewind Festival in August 2025, two months before Ball died; Almond says Ball was in good spirits about the finished record.

content.headline: Jonny Greenwood’s classical curiosity continues to shape his guitar playing
content.shortHeadline: Jonny Greenwood on Steve Reich, Radiohead and learning to play
content.standfirst: As he prepares to perform Steve Reich’s music with the London Sinfonietta, the Radiohead guitarist reflects on the classical influences, arranging choices and daily practice behind his wide-ranging work.

image.caption: Jonny Greenwood, who is performing Steve Reich’s music with the London Sinfonietta.

sources.originalTitle: Jonny Greenwood: ‘In the early days of Radiohead I was a lazy guitar player’

segments.body: Jonny Greenwood is preparing to perform Steve Reich’s music, including “Electric Counterpoint” and “Radio Rewrite,” with the London Sinfonietta. Reich reworked Radiohead material in the latter piece; Greenwood calls that response from a major composer “insanely complimentary.” He has also traced Reich’s influence in Radiohead songs such as “Let Down” and “Weird Fishes/Arpeggi.”

segments.title: The arranger’s ear
segments.body: Greenwood says his role in Radiohead is often less about finding space for a guitar part than about working out what a song needs. He describes Thom Yorke bringing a song such as “Pyramid Song” to the group and the band’s shared task as avoiding anything that would make it worse. He is also preparing a violin concerto and a string quartet.

segments.title: From reluctant player to daily practice
segments.body: Greenwood says he once felt clumsy and lazy as a guitarist, and distrusted technical fluency. Repetition changed that: he now plays guitar every day and says he has become hooked. His musical education also includes the classical composers and analogue synthesizers he encountered before leaving university to tour with Radiohead.

content.headline: Victoria Monét reaches for a sweeping love record on Frequency of Love
content.shortHeadline: Victoria Monét expands her sound on Frequency of Love
content.standfirst: Monét trades some of the playful confidence of Jaguar II for an expansive, often earnest exploration of romance. Pitchfork praises her range while finding that 22 tracks sometimes blur together.

sources.originalTitle: Frequency of Love

segments.body: Frequency of Love stretches Victoria Monét’s polished retro R&B into ballads, interludes and slow jams. The review hears a singer newly willing to state her feelings plainly, with songs that lean into devotion and vulnerability rather than the mischievous persona of her earlier Jaguar records.

segments.title: Ambition and excess
segments.body: Strings, chimes and shifting musical references give the album a cinematic scale. The review singles out “I Want You” for updating quiet storm, and “Reach Out” for its contemporary groove. But at 22 tracks, the project can feel diffuse: similar muted backdrops make some songs run together, and a few guest appearances do little to sharpen Monét’s own distinctive presence.

content.headline: Elvis Costello’s debut gets a revealing, if oversized, anniversary reissue
content.shortHeadline: A vast new set reveals how Elvis Costello found his voice
content.standfirst: A 104-track My Aim Is True edition traces the making of Costello’s 1977 debut through demos, live recordings and alternate versions. Pitchfork finds fresh insight in the scale, despite diminishing returns on its later discs.

sources.originalTitle: My Aim Is True (49th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: The new five-CD My Aim Is True edition puts Costello’s debut in the context of the songs and experiments that came before it. Its demos and early recordings make a case for him as a developing craftsman rather than a sudden, fully formed talent, drawing on American songwriters and pub rock before punk sharpened his public persona.

segments.title: The case for the box
segments.body: The review finds the first two discs especially illuminating: the original album’s sharp, restless songwriting and a collection of earlier material that reveals how it took shape. Later discs, documenting the Attractions and a reunion performance, are more appealing to dedicated fans than essential to the story. The set’s scale is both a pleasure and a reminder of the familiar reissue cycle.

content.headline: Can Ali G still make character comedy work on the big screen?
content.shortHeadline: Ali G’s return tests the future of character comedy
content.standfirst: Sacha Baron Cohen’s new film revives a character built on undercover provocation. Its reception may say as much about the prospects for personality-led cinema as about whether Ali G’s satire still lands.

image.caption: Sacha Baron Cohen as Ali G in Ali G: Who Iz I?

sources.originalTitle: Can Ali G: Who Iz I? save character comedy cinema?

segments.body: Ali G returns in Who Iz I? at a moment when character-led comedy has largely disappeared from cinemas, despite surviving on television through figures such as Alan Partridge and Philomena Cunk. The film’s challenge is twofold: to make its central persona feel relevant again and to show that a comedy built around one performer’s creation can still draw an audience.

segments.title: A changed target
segments.body: The character once satirised the appropriation of Black British culture, but critics have long argued that the joke could also reinforce the caricatures it set out to mock. The article weighs whether Baron Cohen can update Ali G for a more polarised and culturally alert moment, without losing the comic tension that made the character work.

segments.title: A tradition of transformation
segments.body: The piece traces character comedy from Charlie Chaplin and Peter Sellers to Austin Powers and Borat, arguing that disguise and performance can expose the anxieties of a period. It remains uncertain whether Who Iz I? can do that now: the film’s full approach and targets are not yet clear from the material discussed.

content.headline: The Uprising turns the Peasants’ Revolt into a muddled Robin Hood myth
content.shortHeadline: The Uprising’s Peasants’ Revolt becomes a messy Robin Hood tale
content.standfirst: Paul Greengrass brings his handheld urgency to the 1381 revolt, but the film’s invented ploughman and Robin Hood-like coda leave its historical drama unsure of its purpose.

image.caption: Andrew Garfield as the Ploughman in The Uprising.

sources.originalTitle: The Uprising review – Paul Greengrass turns revolutionary rage into a Robin Hood origin myth

segments.body: Paul Greengrass’s The Uprising follows Wat Tyler and John Ball during the 1381 Peasants’ Revolt, alongside an invented ploughman played by Andrew Garfield. The film’s crowded, dirt-caked style gives the rebels’ anger physical force, but its central figure increasingly reads as a Robin Hood precursor rather than a character grounded in the revolt’s history.

segments.title: A coda that undercuts the revolt
segments.body: Cosmo Jarvis and Jamie Bell play Tyler and Ball, while Tom Hollander brings energy to the king’s adviser Sir Robert Hales. The review finds moments to enjoy in the performances, but argues that the ending—Garfield emerging from the forest with his “merry men”—makes the film’s claim about revolutionary legacy feel oddly softened and disappointing.

content.headline: Big Girls Don’t Cry finds tender detail in a teenager’s online double life
content.shortHeadline: Big Girls Don’t Cry is a tender New Zealand coming-of-age film
content.standfirst: Paloma Schneideman’s first feature follows a rural New Zealand teenager in 2006, as online role-playing and real-life friendships complicate her search for identity.

image.caption: Ani Palmer as Sid in Big Girls Don’t Cry.

sources.originalTitle: Big Girls Don’t Cry review – a New Zealand teenager finds herself in tender coming-of-age tale

segments.body: In Big Girls Don’t Cry, 14-year-old Sid spends a summer break drifting between parties, friends and the awkward business of growing up. At times she enters chatrooms and pretends to be someone else; those online games have consequences beyond the screen. The film also follows her gradual recognition of her queerness without making it a lesson or a revelation.

segments.title: A performance built from small moments
segments.body: The review praises Ani Palmer’s restrained, expressive performance and the film’s attentive visual style. Set before smartphones and widespread social media, the story finds enduring weight in ordinary experiences—lounging with friends, trying something for the first time, or watching oneself change—while leaving Sid’s future open.

content.headline: The Social Reckoning puts Facebook on trial—but not beyond Hollywood’s reach
content.shortHeadline: The Social Reckoning puts Facebook on trial, with limits
content.standfirst: Aaron Sorkin’s sequel follows whistleblower Frances Haugen and reporter Jeff Horwitz, but its critics disagree over whether the drama has enough force—and whether Hollywood can mount a genuine challenge to tech power.

image.caption: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.

sources.originalTitle: The Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet Zuckerberg
The Social Reckoning review: Aaron Sorkin's drama puts Facebook on trial, but it won't change anyone's minds ★★☆☆☆
Will the Zuckerberg, Musk and Altman movies make a dent on tech giant evangelism?

segments.body: The Social Reckoning dramatises Frances Haugen’s disclosures about Facebook and the reporting by Jeff Horwitz that followed. The Guardian’s review finds an entertaining, fast-moving thriller, but argues that Mark Zuckerberg—played by Jeremy Strong—is pushed to the margins and that the film avoids naming Trump or confronting how the political landscape has since changed.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s review is more dismissive: it says the film lacks urgency and tension, and that its whistleblower-and-reporter story is too repetitive to change viewers’ minds.

segments.title: Criticism in a compromised industry
segments.body: A separate Guardian analysis places the film alongside projects about Elon Musk and Sam Altman, asking whether studio attention to tech power amounts to a political stance or an opportunistic bet on growing public scepticism. It points to the commercial ties between technology companies and Hollywood as a limit on how freely the industry can criticise its increasingly influential partners.

content.headline: The Lost Children of Tuam tells a painful story without offering easy closure
content.shortHeadline: The Lost Children of Tuam refuses an easy ending
content.standfirst: Monica Dolan plays historian Catherine Corless in a restrained drama about the deaths and unrecorded burials of children at an Irish mother-and-baby home.

image.caption: Monica Dolan as Catherine Corless in The Lost Children of Tuam.

sources.originalTitle: The Lost Children of Tuam review – deeply serious retelling of Ireland’s devastating tragedy

segments.body: Catherine Corless’s local-history research uncovered death certificates for nearly 800 children who died at St Mary’s mother-and-baby home in Tuam, County Galway, without burial records. The film follows Corless as she investigates what happened at the institution, which housed unmarried women and children between 1925 and 1961.

segments.title: No comfort in the final frame
segments.body: The review praises Monica Dolan’s portrayal of Corless and the performances of survivors, while valuing the film’s refusal to make the story feel tidier or more cinematic than it is. It ends without a consoling sense of closure, leaving the weight of what happened—and the absence of graves—unresolved.

content.headline: James Dean’s vulnerability still cuts through the legend
content.shortHeadline: The James Dean worth remembering is more than an icon
content.standfirst: A new screen version of East of Eden renews attention to Dean’s performance as Cal. This piece looks past the pin-up image to the nervous, vulnerable actor who became a star before he was ready for fame.

image.caption: James Dean on the set of Giant in 1955.

sources.originalTitle: The truth about James Dean

segments.body: James Dean’s Cal in Elia Kazan’s East of Eden made him a screen icon, but this account argues that his appeal lies beyond the familiar image of a rebel in a red jacket. The actor brought an exposed, unpredictable quality to the role, especially in the scene where Cal reaches for his father after his birthday gift is rejected.

segments.title: Fame before he was ready
segments.body: The piece recounts Kazan’s decision to work with Dean’s personal history, including his troubled relationship with his father, rather than trying to smooth away his mannerisms. Dean died at 24, after three starring roles, and had described himself as frightened of becoming a film actor. His sudden fame and death helped turn a brief career into a lasting mythology.

content.headline: Sense and Sensibility’s new adaptation makes Austen feel close to the present
content.shortHeadline: Sense and Sensibility finds modern tensions in Austen
content.standfirst: Georgia Oakley’s darker adaptation gives new life to Austen’s sisters and their opposing temperaments. An interview with Fiona Shaw adds insight into the film’s pared-back approach and the career shift that brought her to it.

image.caption: Daisy Edgar-Jones as Elinor Dashwood in Sense and Sensibility.

sources.originalTitle: Every millennial should read Sense and Sensibility
Fiona Shaw: ‘They didn’t think women were funny when I was young’

segments.body: The new Sense and Sensibility follows sisters Elinor and Marianne as they face financial insecurity and the difficult balance between feeling and restraint. The review argues that Austen’s conflict still speaks to a generation negotiating privacy, public self-presentation and uncertain futures, even if this adaptation is less consistent than the 1995 film.

perspectives.body: Fiona Shaw, who plays Mrs Jennings, says director Georgia Oakley wanted a more pared-back version of the character. Shaw describes her as foolish in manner but kind in intention, shaped by the close-knit community in which she grew up.

segments.title: More than a romance
segments.body: The review finds the sisters’ contrasting responses to love particularly legible now: Elinor’s restraint can cost her the man she loves, while Marianne’s romantic certainty obscures warning signs. Shaw, who has appeared in major stage and screen roles, also reflects on a late-career surge after being told as a young actor that she was too old for Hollywood.

content.headline: Frasier’s Niles and Daphne romance still feels like a comedy classic
content.shortHeadline: The Frasier stars look back on Niles and Daphne’s long romance
content.standfirst: Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce revisit the seven-season will-they-won’t-they story, from the tango that became a favourite to the live-audience reaction when the pair finally kissed.

image.caption: Daphne and Niles in Frasier.

sources.originalTitle: ‘He was devastatingly sexy’: Frasier’s Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce on the love between Daphne and Niles

segments.body: Niles Crane’s crush on Daphne Moon began when he first met her in Frasier’s Seattle apartment. Over seven seasons, the show built that attraction into a running romance, delaying its resolution through friendship, misunderstandings and episodes the actors still remember fondly.

segments.title: Timing the payoff
segments.body: Leeves and Hyde Pierce recall rehearsing the tango in “Moon Dance” and the audience’s reaction when Niles and Daphne finally kissed. They say the writers knew when to end the suspense, bringing the characters together before viewers had tired of waiting and giving the series a carefully planned final season.

segments.title: Friends beyond the screen
segments.body: The actors remain close friends, and each speaks warmly about the other’s work and the show’s ensemble. They also reflect on the pregnancy storyline that hid Leeves’s first pregnancy, a choice she says she wishes had been handled differently.

content.headline: Below turns a sea monster into a very silly Newfoundland nightmare
content.shortHeadline: Below is a daft sea-monster horror with a faint climate warning
content.standfirst: Josh Hartnett leads a supernatural thriller about a fishing town, a strange iceberg and a threat from beneath the water. The Guardian review enjoys the pulpy chaos but finds its climate themes submerged.

image.caption: Josh Hartnett as Calvin Penney in Below.

sources.originalTitle: Below review – a killer snot-berg causes chaos for Josh Hartnett

segments.body: Below sends a mysterious iceberg into the harbour of a struggling Newfoundland community. Soon trawlermen are disappearing and body parts are washing ashore; Josh Hartnett plays Calvin Penney, a fisherman whose family history is tied to the town’s earlier maritime tragedies.

segments.title: Monster movie, muted message
segments.body: The review delights in the series’ sea hags, plaid-clad locals and knowingly ridiculous monster premise. It sees hints of a story about warming oceans and a community under pressure, but says those concerns are overwhelmed by the show’s nostalgia, comic gore and creature-feature thrills.

content.headline: Carrie returns as a more sympathetic teen—and divides its reviewers
content.shortHeadline: Carrie’s new series sparks debate over who gets to be a villain
content.standfirst: Mike Flanagan’s eight-part adaptation updates Stephen King’s horror story for social media, but changes to Carrie and her tormentors have divided critics. The debate reaches beyond fidelity to the book to the show’s idea of villainy.

image.caption: Summer H. Howell as Carrie in Mike Flanagan’s series.

sources.originalTitle: Carrie review – the teenage hell-raiser’s glorious return couldn’t come at a better time
Why a new TV version of horror classic Carrie is already annoying people
The Carrie remake made me furious
Cruel torment, depraved violence, evil turns: where did TV’s real baddies go?

segments.body: Mike Flanagan’s Carrie moves Stephen King’s story of a bullied, telekinetic teenager into the present. Summer H. Howell plays Carrie as curious and open to the world after years of home-schooling; the show also gives her mother Margaret and tormentor Chris more context than earlier versions did.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s review finds the added character detail makes the series richer, and sees its focus on online bullying as a reason the story feels relevant now.

segments.title: A question of fidelity—and agency
segments.body: The BBC reports fans’ objections to Carrie’s casting and characterisation, while also citing a horror scholar who argues that the series codes her outsider status in other ways. The i Paper’s reviewer objects more strongly, arguing that the changes drain Carrie of agency and make her revenge less satisfying.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s reviewer, who describes King’s novel as a personal touchstone, sees the adaptation as a fundamental loss of Carrie’s anger and independence, not simply a modernising choice.

segments.title: The case for frightening villains
segments.body: A wider argument about recent screen villains places Carrie alongside East of Eden and the drama War. It questions a trend toward giving antagonists sympathetic explanations for their behaviour, asking whether empathy can sometimes soften the force of horror and drama.

content.headline: Bake Off’s audience-choice week brings a welcome pinch of chaos
content.shortHeadline: Bake Off shakes up its cosy formula with audience choice
content.standfirst: The first audience-set challenges handed power to viewers rather than judges Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood. The result was not outright mayhem, but the show’s new tension and unpredictability pleased this critic.

image.caption: Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood judge The Great British Bake Off.

sources.originalTitle: Bake Off is toughening up. Good

segments.body: For the first time, Great British Bake Off viewers chose the week’s challenges. The bakers made cheesecakes with family members, faced individual technical tasks using a basic-ingredient cupboard, and were asked to create wearable bakes. The critic sees the experiment as a welcome disruption to the programme’s familiar cosy formula.

segments.title: A little more edge
segments.body: The challenges produced some mishaps, while the judges’ sharper exchanges brought a different energy to the tent. The review notes that Paul Hollywood did not soften his criticism when a cake collapsed, and that Lawson was willing to disagree with him. It argues the series can keep its warmth while allowing more friction and surprise.

content.headline: Richard Armitage finds a new kind of intensity in crime drama Winter
content.shortHeadline: Richard Armitage on playing forensic pathologist Ethan Winter
content.standfirst: The actor discusses his latest ITV role, his attraction to dark characters and the private life he chooses to keep off screen, alongside the uneasy comic edge of his forensic pathologist.

image.caption: Richard Armitage, who plays forensic pathologist Ethan Winter.

sources.originalTitle: Winter’s Richard Armitage: ‘My pillow humping scene was improvised’

segments.body: In ITV’s Winter, Richard Armitage plays forensic pathologist Ethan Winter, who addresses murder victims before examining them. Armitage says he enjoyed building a slow-burn relationship between Winter and DI Bell, while recognising that the pathologist’s confidence and mansplaining can make him obnoxious.

segments.title: The pull of extreme roles
segments.body: Armitage says he is drawn to characters who explore grief, terror and violence, and that directors often tell him to pull back after he has pushed a scene far. He also revisits the improvised pillow scene in Obsession, explaining that it was intended to feel degrading and tragic, not erotic.

segments.title: Keeping a private life
segments.body: The actor says he values the distinction between public work and personal life, and does not think performers should have to share everything. He also describes writing novels and narrating audiobooks as ways to enter the focused state he once sought through learning the cello.

content.headline: Amy Dowden’s early Strictly exit raises questions about partner choices
content.shortHeadline: Amy Dowden deserved more than another early Strictly exit
content.standfirst: A second week-one elimination in a row leaves the professional dancer without the chance to build a partnership this series. This critic argues that the show’s pairing choices have repeatedly denied her a proper run.

image.caption: Amy Dowden, who left Strictly Come Dancing in the first week for a second year running.

sources.originalTitle: Amy Dowden’s exit exposes one big Strictly problem

segments.body: Amy Dowden and celebrity hairdresser Chris Appleton left Strictly Come Dancing in the first week. The critic argues that the professional dancer’s popularity and skill deserved a better chance to develop a partnership, especially after a run of difficult series marked by illness, injury and an earlier early exit.

segments.title: The professionals are the draw
segments.body: The piece argues that audiences often invest in the relationships between professionals and celebrities more than the celebrity’s pre-existing fame. It sees Dowden as a central part of the programme’s sense of community and says she deserved a series defined by her work as a dancer and mentor, rather than another story of resilience through hardship.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s future is uncertain after the Disney+ partnership ends
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain future after Disney+ exit
content.standfirst: The BBC has ended its collaboration with Disney+, cancelled a planned Christmas special and is seeking a new funding partner. Fans and observers disagree on what went wrong, but fear the series may remain off screen.

image.caption: Several actors who have played the Doctor, including Ncuti Gatwa and Jodie Whittaker.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Doctor Who has no announced next Doctor, its planned Christmas special has been cancelled, and the BBC is seeking a company to help fund future productions after ending its Disney+ partnership. No new backer has emerged in the material gathered, and the BBC has declined to comment further on the show’s future.

segments.title: How a television institution lost momentum
segments.body: The article traces the series’ revival in 2005, its changing Doctors and showrunners, and the online abuse that greeted Jodie Whittaker and Ncuti Gatwa. Interviewees disagree about the causes of declining interest, pointing to scripts, the scale of Disney+’s investment and how the latest era handled the central character.

segments.title: A pause, or a longer silence?
segments.body: Fans interviewed for the piece accept that long-running shows sometimes need a break, but worry that Doctor Who could become an archive rather than a continuing series. Its future remains unsettled; one of the show’s former writers describes the programme’s values as kindness and curiosity, while fans say they want it back on screen.

content.headline: The Split Up brings a British Asian family to a new legal drama
content.shortHeadline: The Split Up takes its family-law drama to Manchester
content.standfirst: Ritu Arya and Sanjeev Bhaskar lead the new spin-off, which keeps The Split’s tangled relationships while centring a predominantly British Asian cast and creative team.

image.caption: Ritu Arya in The Split Up.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: The Split Up moves the family-law drama from London to Manchester, where Ritu Arya plays barrister Aria Kishan, poised to take over her father Dhruv’s firm. A death in the family, a change in succession plans and the return of a former flame set up the show’s legal and personal conflicts.

segments.title: Everyday lives on screen
segments.body: Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted to create British Asian characters living ordinary lives, rather than treating representation as a series of exceptional or stereotyped circumstances. The show’s creative team is also predominantly British Asian, an approach the article describes as still unusual in mainstream British television.

perspectives.body: Executive producer Abi Morgan says the spin-off retains the original show’s central mix of family, ambition, betrayal and romantic entanglement, while giving a new writing team room to shape its own version.

content.headline: GTA 6’s £350 collector’s box reflects a widening gaming price divide
content.shortHeadline: GTA 6’s £350 merch box points to gaming’s price divide
content.standfirst: Rockstar’s collector’s box costs more than the game and does not include it. The Guardian’s games columnist sees the price as part of a wider trend that risks making console gaming a luxury hobby.

image.caption: Rockstar’s Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection.

sources.originalTitle: What the £350 Grand Theft Auto ‘collector’s box’ says about the escalating cost of gaming

segments.body: Rockstar’s Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection costs £350 and contains merchandise, but not the game itself. With the game listed at £70, a player wanting both would pay £420. The columnist says the price is unusually high even by the standards of costly gaming special editions.

segments.title: A market split
segments.body: The article argues that premium consoles, games and merchandise increasingly target the players able to spend most. It contrasts that market with the much larger number of people who play free or low-cost mobile games, and warns that physical games are becoming harder to find and buy second-hand.

segments.title: More than collecting
segments.body: The writer is not dismissive of collectors—he cherishes some special editions himself—but sees the price as a sign of who the industry expects to spend. His concern is that games built as substantial worlds, rather than short diversions, may become less accessible as costs rise and physical copies grow scarce.

content.headline: Silver Pines is a stylish detective game built for noir immersion
content.shortHeadline: Silver Pines is a stylish, atmospheric detective adventure
content.standfirst: A private eye searches a deserted town for a missing singer-songwriter in this 2D adventure. Its familiar puzzles and tense combat are lifted by striking design, careful pacing and a rich noir atmosphere.

image.caption: Silver Pines, a detective adventure set in a deserted town.

sources.originalTitle: Silver Pines review – a stylish, neo-noir detective drama

segments.body: Silver Pines casts players as private detective Red Walker, searching a deserted town for a missing musician. Payphones offer clues and save points; newspapers, statues and other objects unlock rooms and push the mystery forward. The review finds the point-and-click structure familiar, with survival-horror combat that makes ammunition and fragile weapons feel precious.

segments.title: A world worth getting lost in
segments.body: Rotoscoped animation, neon signs, shifting shadows and detailed interiors give the game a distinctive film-noir look. Its soundtrack evokes sleazy jazz and cinematic unease, while references to Twin Peaks, Blue Velvet and other screen works deepen the atmosphere. Puzzles can be obscure, but the reviewer relishes exploring and piecing together the town’s mythology.

content.headline: Gears of War: E-Day has thrilling combat but too little else
content.shortHeadline: Gears of War: E-Day’s excellent combat can’t save its repetition
content.standfirst: The prequel delivers the series’ most satisfying fighting, but recycled routes, sprawling objectives and intrusive collectibles leave the rest of the campaign feeling overlong and short of ideas.

image.caption: Marcus Fenix in Gears of War: E-Day.

sources.originalTitle: Gears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring

segments.body: E-Day returns to the alien invasion that defined the Gears of War series, following Marcus Fenix and three other soldiers through the first days of the attack. The opening gives the invasion scale and menace, but the review says the campaign keeps returning players to the same streets and bridge crossings without developing its ideas.

segments.title: The series at its best—and its most frustrating
segments.body: Combat feels better than in previous entries, with weighty weapons, destructible environments and more fluid movement between cover. But large areas are cluttered with collectibles and side activities, while the game can punish exploration with a mission failure. The reviewer finds the contrast especially jarring when a collectible chime interrupts an emotional scene.

content.headline: Resident Evil’s new film recreates the fear of playing the games
content.shortHeadline: The new Resident Evil film captures the games’ survival-horror feel
content.standfirst: Rather than rely on familiar heroes, Zach Cregger’s adaptation follows an ordinary courier through a nightmare of scarce ammunition, strange clues and hostile spaces—the rhythms of playing Resident Evil itself.

image.caption: Zach Cregger on the set of the new Resident Evil film.

sources.originalTitle: How Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil stands out from all other game adaptations

segments.body: Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil has no Leon, Claire or Ada Wong. Instead, it follows courier Bryan Hodukavich as a virus outbreak traps him in Raccoon City with little ammunition and no clear sense of what is happening. The film moves through settings familiar to players, from an abandoned farmhouse and car-filled tunnel to a hospital and sewer.

segments.title: A player’s point of view
segments.body: The article argues that the adaptation’s fidelity lies less in reproducing the games’ famous characters than in recreating their mechanics: found recordings, terse encounters with non-player characters, limited supplies and an uncertain path through escalating danger. It connects the approach to a wider set of films that explore how games make audiences feel like participants in unfamiliar worlds.

content.headline: Ace Combat 8 delivers a thrilling fighter-pilot fantasy
content.shortHeadline: Ace Combat 8 makes the Top Gun fantasy soar
content.standfirst: Dogfights, dramatic music and spectacular skies deliver the arcade flight series’ familiar rush. A more fully realised story adds emotional weight, though the battlefields can become visually confusing.

image.caption: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve puts players in the cockpit of a fighter jet.

sources.originalTitle: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve review – brilliant aerial combat game fulfils the Top Gun fantasy

segments.body: Ace Combat 8 puts players in the role of a pilot whose invented reputation becomes real as a besieged nation looks for a hero. The game mixes accessible flight controls with expert options, and offers missions ranging from escort work to attacks on a railgun-equipped land battleship and radar-invisible aircraft.

segments.title: A bigger story in the air
segments.body: The review praises the game’s cloudscapes, forceful score and more cinematic character scenes, saying they make the squad and its conflict feel more immediate than in the previous instalment. Its story borrows from Top Gun, but the critic says the emotional effect lands. In combat, however, objectives can be hard to pick out amid visual clutter.

segments.title: A triumphant return
segments.body: Environmental destruction and new ways to interact with wing-mates expand the formula without replacing its central appeal: fast, theatrical dogfights. The reviewer could not test the online multiplayer mode during the review period, but judges the single-player game a success despite that limitation.

content.headline: GTA 6’s virtual romance is exposing real relationship anxieties
content.shortHeadline: GTA 6’s romance debate is about more than video games
content.standfirst: Online claims that tending to an in-game couple counts as cheating have prompted ridicule and serious discussion alike. The debate reveals wider unease about attention, loneliness and what partners owe one another.

image.caption: GTA VI protagonists Lucia and Jason.

sources.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner?

segments.body: In GTA VI, players can strengthen the relationship between Lucia and Jason by spending time together, texting and going on dates. Some social-media users argue that playing these interactions amounts to “micro-cheating,” prompting counterarguments that the game’s virtual romance is being mistaken for a real one.

segments.title: The feeling beneath the argument
segments.body: The article warns against dismissing every complaint as jealousy. It suggests that a partner may feel hurt if someone invests care and attention in a fictional relationship while neglecting a real one, particularly amid loneliness and disconnection. It also notes that the game’s dating mechanic is not new: romance has been a feature of games for decades.

segments.title: Boundaries, not a universal rule
segments.body: The writer personally does not consider in-game romance cheating, but acknowledges that couples can set different boundaries. The argument is less about a definitive rule than about what the unexpected controversy says about dissatisfaction and unmet needs in real relationships.

content.headline: The White House’s gaming arcade turns play into migrant-bashing propaganda
content.shortHeadline: The White House arcade weaponises familiar video-game styles
content.standfirst: A set of mini-games on the US government’s website borrows from familiar titles to promote hostile messages about migrants. The piece argues that the appropriation of gaming culture deserves attention beyond the immediate outrage.

image.caption: A screenshot from the White House Arcade game Build the Wall.

sources.originalTitle: The Trump White House’s fetish for gamer culture has moved up a level with new arcade

segments.body: The White House has published an arcade of mini-games that riffs on familiar titles. Among them, Build the Wall turns a Tetris-like format into a border game, while Rio Run asks players to patrol the Rio Grande and collect people depicted in orange jumpsuits. The article calls these games dehumanising and mean-spirited.

segments.title: A political language borrowed from games
segments.body: The piece situates the arcade within a broader effort by the Trump administration to use gaming imagery in political messaging, following earlier references to Halo and Pokémon. Games scholar George Osborn argues that the far right’s use of gaming culture has moved beyond social posts toward attempts to draw audiences into the medium itself.

perspectives.body: Osborn describes the arcade as an escalation: a shift from appropriating video-game culture on social media to using games themselves to try to reach audiences.

segments.title: Outrage is part of the design
segments.body: The writer says the mini-games are unlikely to persuade people who do not already support the administration, and warns that outrage can itself become part of their intended attention strategy. But the games’ existence still raises questions about how play can be weaponised, especially as political and commercial interests grow more deeply entangled with the industry.

content.headline: Mobile game adverts lead one player into a grim algorithmic rabbit hole
content.shortHeadline: A mobile-game ad binge descends into algorithmic sludge
content.standfirst: A columnist’s attempt to use quick phone games as a break becomes a parade of intrusive ads, dubious downloads and increasingly personal pitches. The result is a funny, uneasy account of freemium design.

image.caption: A screenshot from the mobile game Annoying Uncle Punch.

sources.originalTitle: Help! I have disappeared down a rabbithole of horrible mobile gaming adverts

segments.body: Trying to take a short break with mobile games, the writer begins with a simple free-to-play title that limits attempts unless players wait or watch ads. Each ad points to another game, many of which promise features that are absent once downloaded or make further advertising unavoidable.

segments.title: From game recommendations to grifts
segments.body: The sequence moves from cheap mobile games to ads for slot machines, supposed cash rewards and personal products. Some ads cannot be skipped easily, and attempts to alter preferences or open privacy information fail. The writer compares the experience to being trapped in a funnel designed to keep attention and extract money.

content.headline: UK teenager receives pioneering transplant of his frozen testicular tissue
content.shortHeadline: A first UK testicular tissue transplant offers hope, not certainty
